You will apply Kirchhoff's current law at a node and Kirchhoff's voltage law around a loop. These laws let you write equations for a circuit that cannot be reduced by inspection.

**Used in college or university:** Nodal analysis, mesh analysis, electronics, power systems, and control hardware. [[1, Ch. 9]](../../references.qmd#ref-grob2016)

**Where you see it:** In a car wiring harness, current splits between lights and control modules. In a robot, it splits between the controller, sensors, and motors.

::: {.callout-note title="Reference and polarity"}
The bottom rail is normally the 0 V or ground reference, and higher-voltage nodes are drawn above it. On a vertical battery symbol, the long line is positive. Keep that polarity consistent with every current arrow and voltage sign when writing Kirchhoff equations.
:::

## Kirchhoff's current law

<figure class="ter-circuit-figure" id="fig-kirchhoff-node-loop" data-diagram-source="../../assets/electronics/schematics/kirchhoff-node-loop-reference.tex">
<img src="../../assets/electronics/schematics/kirchhoff-current-law-node.svg" alt="Square junction node with one entering current and three leaving currents." loading="lazy">
<figcaption><a class="ter-figure-label" href="#fig-kirchhoff-node-loop">Figure 1.</a> At a square junction node, total current entering equals total current leaving. <a class="ter-figure-anchor" href="#fig-kirchhoff-node-loop" aria-label="Link to Figure 1">#</a></figcaption>
</figure>

$$
\sum I_{\mathrm{in}} = \sum I_{\mathrm{out}}
$$ {#eq-kirchhoff-current}

A negative answer means the real current is opposite the arrow you selected.

## Kirchhoff's voltage law

<figure class="ter-circuit-figure" id="fig-kirchhoff-two-loop" data-diagram-source="../../assets/electronics/schematics/kirchhoff-node-loop-reference.tex">
<img src="../../assets/electronics/schematics/kirchhoff-two-loop-network.svg" alt="Two-loop circuit with two sources, three resistors, square nodes, and labelled currents." loading="lazy">
<figcaption><a class="ter-figure-label" href="#fig-kirchhoff-two-loop">Figure 2.</a> Two loops share one resistor and create two simultaneous equations. <a class="ter-figure-anchor" href="#fig-kirchhoff-two-loop" aria-label="Link to Figure 2">#</a></figcaption>
</figure>

$$
\sum_{k=1}^{n}\Delta V_k = 0
$$ {#eq-kirchhoff-voltage}

Choose one loop direction and keep the signs consistent. A source rise is positive; a resistor drop in the current direction is negative.

## Workflow

1. Mark the essential nodes and independent loops.
2. Choose and label unknown current directions.
3. Write current-law and voltage-law equations.
4. Replace resistor voltage with $V=IR$.
5. Solve without rounding, then check every original node and loop equation.
6. Build the same network in Tinkercad and compare the simulated values.

## Worked solutions {#worked-solutions}

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Question 2: Missing loop voltage"}
Kirchhoff's voltage law requires the source rise to equal the voltage drops:

$$
V_3=12.0\,\mathrm{V}-2.4\,\mathrm{V}-4.1\,\mathrm{V}=5.5\,\mathrm{V}.
$$ {#eq-kirchhoff-worked-q2-voltage}

**Check:** $12.0-2.4-4.1-5.5=0.0\,\mathrm{V}$.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Question 4: Two loops with two sources"}
The two loop equations are

$$
5I_1-2I_2=10
$$ {#eq-kirchhoff-worked-q4-left-loop}

$$
-2I_1+7I_2=6.
$$ {#eq-kirchhoff-worked-q4-right-loop}

Solving them gives $I_1=2.645161\ldots\,\mathrm{mA}$ and $I_2=1.612903\ldots\,\mathrm{mA}$.

The shared-branch current is

$$
I_3=I_1-I_2=1.032258\ldots\,\mathrm{mA}.
$$ {#eq-kirchhoff-worked-q4-shared-current}

**Final answers:** $I_1=2.65\,\mathrm{mA}$, $I_2=1.61\,\mathrm{mA}$, and $I_3=1.03\,\mathrm{mA}$.
:::

## Practical pathway: test the node and loops

**Core learning:** derive the node and loop equations by hand before using a simulator or solver. Follow **Define Variables → Write Equations → Standard Form or Matrix → Solve → Verify**.

**Guided practice:** if Tinkercad can represent the same sources and passive components faithfully, build the two-loop network with the [Tinkercad tutorial](tinkercad-circuits.qmd). Otherwise, use the teacher-approved physical circuit or simulator and identify the substitution. Measure the currents needed for one KCL check and voltages needed for one KVL check.

| Check | Predicted total | Simulated or measured total | Residual |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Current entering minus leaving (mA) | 0 |  |  |
| Left-loop voltage sum (V) | 0 |  |  |
| Right-loop voltage sum (V) | 0 |  |  |

**Independent challenge:** deliberately reverse one current arrow without changing the circuit. Rewrite the affected signs, solve again, and explain why a negative result is meaningful rather than automatically wrong.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Progressive hints"}
1. Keep one chosen loop direction from start to finish.
2. Compare every matrix row with its original KCL or KVL equation.
3. A residual near zero checks the entered equations; compare signs and units with the schematic to check the model.
:::

Use [Notebook 3](../../assets/tej-computational/notebooks/03-kirchhoff-systems.ipynb) only after deriving the equations. Record the coefficient order and verify by substitution.

**Reflection:** What did the residual establish, and what mistake could still produce a near-zero residual?
